slides.body:
The Hindenburg Disaster — 1937

Watch the clip. What do you notice?
slides.notes: Play the Hindenburg clip (2:29–3:31). Ask: What happened? How did it make you feel? What do you know about the Hindenburg? Introduce the topic of historical events.

slides.title: What just happened?
slides.body:
What did you see?

Why do you think the Hindenburg is still remembered today?

What other historical events do you know about?
slides.notes: Elicit reactions. Guide: The Hindenburg was a German airship that exploded in 1937. It was filmed and shown in newsreels around the world — one of the first media disasters.

slides.title: Adverbs of Manner
slides.notes: Transition: Now let's learn how to describe HOW something happens. Adverbs of manner. Play audio track 1.25.

slides.body:
Listen and repeat

badlybeautifully
bravelycarefully
greedilyheavily
quicklyslowly
slides.notes: Play the audio track 1.25. Define each word as a class. Elicit the base adjective for each adverb (slow → slowly, careful → carefully).

slides.title: Adjective → Adverb
slides.body: slow→slowly
slides.notes: Step 1: Show 'slow' (light italic serif) and 'slowly' (bold uppercase sans-serif) with an arrow. Ask: What's the difference? (adjective vs adverb)

slides.title: slow + -ly = slowly
slides.body:
slowly

The snail moved slowly across the path.

Adjective: slow (describes a noun)
Adverb: slowly (describes a verb — how something happens)
slides.notes: Step 2: 'slow' and 'slowly' merge as 'slowly' in gold with the snail image. Explain: slow (adj) describes a noun. Slowly (adv) describes a verb — how something happens. Add -ly to most adjectives to make adverbs.

slides.title: Structured Discourse
slides.body:
**1. Opinion** — What do you think?

**2. Reason** — Why do you think that?

**3. Story** — Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?
slides.notes: Explain: When you speak for a minute, follow this structure. Opinion → Reason → Story/Example. Let's practice by listening to a model.

slides.title: Model — The Hindenburg Disaster
slides.body: I think one of the most dramatic historical events was the Hindenburg disaster of 1937. Why? Because it was one of the first times a major disaster was captured on film and shown in newsreels all over the world. For example, thousands of people watched the newsreel in movie theaters. They saw the giant airship burst into flames in just 34 seconds. Another reason is that it changed the future of travel forever. Before the Hindenburg, people believed airships were the future of long-distance travel. After the disaster, the age of airships ended completely. So this event shows us how technology can change in an instant, and how one moment can change history. When you speak, try to follow this structure: give your opinion, explain your reason, and share an example.
slides.notes: Play the audio model. Point out the natural structure: Opinion (most dramatic event) → Reason (captured on film) → Example (newsreels, 34 seconds) → Another reason (changed travel forever) → Conclusion. Ask students to prepare a similar 1-minute talk about a historical event.

slides.body:
Exercise 2

Agree (A) or disagree (D)? Discuss why.

1Stopping the spread of disease is more important than space exploration.
2There will always be wars.
3The development of flight changed the world forever.
4All inventions and discoveries are good.
slides.notes: Students discuss in pairs or groups. Walk around and monitor. After 5 minutes, elicit some opinions. Use opinion language: I think... / In my opinion... / I agree because...

slides.title: Questions?
slides.body: Any questions about what we've learned today?
slides.notes: Wrap up. Ask: What new words can you use to talk about world events? What's the difference between an adjective and an adverb? Which information source do you find most useful for learning history?
